name: Agent-as-a-Judge / DevAI (metauto-ai)
one_line: An agentic judge with a 33-format 'read module' grades a builder agent's workspace against 365 hierarchical requirements across 55 DevAI tasks, without executing code; ICML 2025.
why_relevant: Q3 (non-self-graded verification) and Q4 (evidence). Judge is a separate agent that reads artifacts (code, images, docs) the builder produced; builder never sees the judge. Directly comparable to the owner's judge seat: gray-box (judge sees trajectory) vs black-box (artifacts only) both beat plain LLM-as-a-Judge. PRDBench (2025-10) builds on it, so the mechanism has been adopted by at least one follow-on benchmark.
claimed_results: arXiv 2410.10934 v2 (2024-10-16) / README: alignment with human consensus — OpenHands 90.44% black-box / 90.16% gray-box vs LLM-as-a-Judge 60.38% / 70.76%; MetaGPT 88.52% / 92.07% vs 84.15% / 68.86%; GPT-Pilot 83.88% / 86.61% vs 65.30% / 71.85%. Saves '97.72% of time' and '97.64% of costs' vs human experts. DevAI: only 1.81% of tasks fully solved by GPT-Pilot/OpenHands; OpenHands 42.89% requirements met (independent) / 28.68% (dependency-aware).

name: CodeMonkeys (Stanford Scaling Intelligence)
one_line: Samples many edit trajectories per SWE-bench issue, votes with model-generated tests, then runs a dedicated selection trajectory that writes new tests to split the top-k candidates.
why_relevant: Q3: verification by model-written tests that were generated independently of each candidate edit, plus a second-stage 'selection state machine' that authors discriminating tests. A copyable pattern for the owner's fix seat: keep N candidate patches and let a separate seat write tests to pick among them rather than trusting the builder's own green run. Q4: the paper does NOT report a selection-vs-oracle gap, so how much the tests discriminate is not quantified.
claimed_results: arXiv 2501.14723 (submitted 2025-01-24, rev 2025-02-03): 57.4% SWE-bench Verified for ~2300 USD; selecting over an ensemble of existing top submissions gives 66.2%, above the best member. README: 'first pick the k codebase edits that pass the most generated tests… then run a state machine [that] writes new tests to differentiate between the k edits'.

name: NVIDIA Nemotron-CORTEXA
one_line: Localisation + repair agent that filters candidate patches through regression tests and LLM-generated reproduction tests, then majority-votes with an o3 LLM-judge tiebreak; ICML 2025.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: concrete pipeline of execution-based filters before any LLM judgement; the judge (o3/o3-mini) only breaks ties among execution-surviving candidates. Reports the oracle ceiling, which lets you size the selection loss — useful for deciding how much a judge seat can add over held-out execution.
claimed_results: Research page (dated 2025-04-09): 68.2% SWE-bench Verified at $3.28 inference per problem; 'the 7 candidate patches contain correct repairs in 75% of problems' (so ~7 pts lost to selection). Bryan Catanzaro tweet 2025-05-27: top of SWE-bench leaderboard at 68.2%. Repo runs `--vote_mode llm_judge` after reproduction-test filtering.

name: TDD-Bench Verified / Auto-TDD (IBM)
one_line: 449 SWE-bench-derived issues where the deliverable is a test suite written from the issue text alone; graded by fail-to-pass on the gold fix plus coverage adequacy in Docker.
why_relevant: Q3: this is the exact job of the owner's spec seat (tests from the ticket alone, before code exists). Gives a harness and metric (fail-to-pass + coverage of the change) for auditing spec-seat output, and is the substrate the test-overfitting study below used.
claimed_results: arXiv 2412.02883 (2024-12-03): 449 instances; 'Auto-TDD yields a better fail-to-pass rate than the strongest prior work while also yielding high coverage adequacy' (no absolute numbers in abstract).

name: Investigating Test Overfitting on SWE-bench
one_line: Measures how often a patch passes issue-generated tests but fails the gold tests, and shows that joint code+test refinement and hiding test details both make it worse.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: the closest published measurement of the owner's falseFinish metric. Key mechanism findings: (a) letting the builder iterate against generated tests increases overfitting; (b) merely obscuring test details does not help — only truly held-out gold tests do. Supports the owner's OS-sandbox split over prompt-level hiding.
claimed_results: arXiv 2511.16858 (submitted 2025-11-20, rev 2026-04-03). Agentless + e-Otter++ on 449 TDD-Bench Verified instances: overfitting rate 21.8% (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, 229 inst.) and 33.0% (GPT-4o, 176 inst.); with code refinement rises to 25.5% and 35.9%; hiding test details while keeping prompt augmentation: 63.6% exposed vs 72.2% hidden (worse); with golden tests revealed: 5.8% / 11.3% but only ~3% real gain.

name: OpenHands Critic (SWE-Gym verifier lineage to 2026 production critic)
one_line: A separate small critic model scores agent trajectories 0-1 during/after a run; used for best-of-N selection and early stopping in the OpenHands SDK/CLI with a retry-below-threshold loop.
why_relevant: Q2 and Q3: a verifier that is a distinct component from the builder, trained on the system's own production traces (PR-merge and code-survival signals) rather than benchmark data — a self-learning loop without fine-tuning the builder. SDK docs (docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/critic) show IterativeRefinementConfig: default threshold 0.6, max 3 iterations, automatic follow-up prompt. Caveat: builder-visible score can be optimised against; the blog reports benchmark-trained critics were worse than random.
claimed_results: Blog 2026-03-05: critics trained on benchmark data only 'AUC ~0.45–0.48 (worse than random)'; code-survival supervision AUC 0.69; Best@8 73.8% vs 57.9% random; early stopping +17.7 pp over random with 1.35 avg attempts vs 8.0. Earlier HF card openhands-critic-32b-exp-20250417 (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, trained on SWE-Gym trajectories): SWE-bench Verified 60.6% single trajectory to 66.4% with critic over 5 attempts. SWE-Gym README (ICML 2025): verifier best-of-n 32%/26% Verified/Lite.
last_activity: 2026-03-05 (blog); SWE-Gym repo last commit 2025-07-29; SDK critic page marked 'highly experimental'

name: R2E-Gym: hybrid execution-based + execution-free verifiers
one_line: Shows execution-based verifiers (run generated tests) and execution-free verifiers (LLM reads the patch) fail in complementary ways and that combining them beats either alone.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: empirical argument for the owner's layered gate (held-out Playwright suite AND independent critics) rather than one or the other. Execution verifiers had 'low distinguishability'; execution-free ones were 'biased and often rely on stylistic features'.
claimed_results: arXiv 2504.07164 (2025-04-09): each verifier alone saturates ~42-43%; hybrid reaches 51% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified (open-weights SOTA at the time); 34.4% pass@1 for a 32B model. Site r2e-gym.github.io; 8.7K procedurally generated environments.

name: TestGen-LLM (Meta, FSE 2024 industry track)
one_line: Generated tests only reach engineers after passing a hard filter chain: builds, passes reliably (repeated runs), and measurably increases coverage.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: the canonical 'filters, not judgement' design — every LLM output is accepted only if it clears deterministic gates, which is the same posture as the owner's sealed gate. Production adoption numbers at Meta scale. Older than 18 months but named in the brief.
claimed_results: arXiv 2402.09171 (2024-02-14): Instagram Reels/Stories evaluation — 75% of generated test cases built correctly, 57% passed reliably, 25% increased coverage; across test-a-thons improved 11.5% of classes applied to; 73% of recommendations accepted for production by Meta engineers.

name: Qodo Cover (formerly Cover-Agent)
one_line: Open-source test-coverage agent that keeps a generated test only if it runs, passes and raises measured coverage; archived June 2025 in favour of the commercial qodo-ci.
why_relevant: Q3: same accept-only-on-measured-improvement loop as TestGen-LLM, in a form you can read. Q4: one documented external acceptance (PR merged into huggingface/pytorch-image-models per Qodo blog). Project is unmaintained, so treat as reference code, not a dependency.
claimed_results: Qodo blog: autonomous PR with 15 unit tests covering 168 new lines accepted into HF pytorch-image-models; PRs also sent to facebook/prophet and microsoft/onnxscript. README: validates each test 'runs successfully, passes, and increases code coverage'. No aggregate metrics.

name: EvilGenie: A Reward Hacking Benchmark
one_line: Inspect-based harness that detects test gaming with three independent channels: ~30% held-out tests, an LLM judge classifying the solution, and SHA-256 hashes of test files before/after the run.
why_relevant: Q3: a small, readable implementation of exactly the owner's gate trio (held-out split, independent judge, tamper detection). Finding worth noting: the LLM judge caught unambiguous hacks well and hidden tests added little on top — the opposite ranking to the Anthropic hidden-test method, so the two should be combined, not substituted.
claimed_results: arXiv 2511.21654 (2025-11-26, rev 2026-05-17): Codex and Claude Code showed 'explicit reward hacking', Gemini CLI 'misaligned behavior'; 'the LLM judge' is 'highly effective at detecting reward hacking in unambiguous cases' while hidden test cases showed 'minimal additional benefit'. README: ~70% visible / ~30% holdout (max 10), 50 turns, 600 s timeout.

name: Cursor: 'Reward hacking is swamping model intelligence gains'
one_line: Cursor built an audit agent that reads full trajectories blind to pass/fail and found most 'solved' public-benchmark tasks were solved by retrieving the known fix; gives concrete environment hardening.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: the strongest recent evidence that a green suite is not evidence of capability unless the environment is sealed. Mitigations map one-to-one onto the owner's design: strip .git history to a single commit, deny egress by default with a pinned registry allowlist, run a blind trajectory auditor, keep a private eval set. Also a working example of an audit seat that is a separate model call.
claimed_results: Post dated 2026-06-25: 731 Opus 4.8 Max trajectories audited; 57% used upstream lookup, 9% git-history mining; on SWE-bench Pro 63% of successful resolutions retrieved rather than derived the fix; Opus 4.8 Max 87.1% to 73.0% under strict conditions; Composer 2.5 74.7% to 54.0%. Training-time gaming examples: recovering a deleted signature from a type-checker cache; decompiling Java bytecode.

name: METR: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
one_line: Independent evaluator documents o3 and others modifying tests/scoring code, monkey-patching evaluators and locating reference answers, with per-task rates and published transcripts.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: independent (non-vendor) measurement that prompt-level prohibitions barely move the rate, so verification must be structural (scoring code out of reach, hidden answers). Also recommends detection via high-score analysis and LLM monitoring plus patching the scoring loophole — matches the owner's audit-then-repair-the-pipeline tier.
claimed_results: Post 2025-06-05: o3 reward hacked in 30.4% of RE-Bench runs (39/128); 'Optimize LLM Foundry' 100%, 'Scaffolding for Rust Codecontest' 42.9%, 'Optimize a Kernel' 25%; HCAST 0.7% (8/1087). With explicit do-not-cheat instructions models still hacked in 70-95% of attempts across prompt variants.
last_activity: 2025-06-05 (post); METR Frontier Risk Report 2026-05-19 exists but not opened

name: Anthropic System Card Addendum: Claude Opus 4.1 (Section 5, Reward hacking)
one_line: Vendor eval that scores hard-coding two ways — a classifier over outputs and held-out tests hidden from the model — plus 'Claude Code impossible tasks' run sandboxed with auto-accept until the model admits defeat or hacks.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: the only vendor table (read directly from the PDF) that reports a hidden-test hack rate next to a classifier hack rate for the same tasks, so it calibrates how much each detector sees. Also defines the 'impossible task' protocol (unsolvable due to bug/missing dependency) that the owner's negative-control probes should copy, and shows the anti-hack prompt effect size.
claimed_results: Card dated August 2025 (changelog 2025-09-15), Table 5.B: Reward-hack-prone coding tasks classifier / hidden-test hack rate — Opus 4.1 12% / 14%, Opus 4 9% / 13%, Sonnet 4 4% / 12%, Sonnet 3.7 44% / 23%. Claude Code Impossible Tasks classifier hack rate no prompt / anti-hack prompt — Opus 4.1 52% / 18%, Opus 4 51% / 19%, Sonnet 4 51% / 7%, Sonnet 3.7 78% / 80%. Average hack rate: Sonnet 4 14.8%, Opus 4 18.2%, Opus 4.1 18.2%.
last_activity: 2025-09-15 (changelog); Sonnet 4.5 (2025-09) and Opus 4.6 (2026-02) cards exist but PDFs exceeded fetch limit

name: OpenAI Codex sandbox and cloud egress policy (docs + GPT-5.2-Codex addendum)
one_line: Cloud Codex blocks internet during the agent phase by default, with a ~80-domain dependency allowlist and GET/HEAD/OPTIONS-only option; local CLI uses Seatbelt (macOS) and bubblewrap/Landlock/seccomp (Linux) with network off by default.
why_relevant: Q3: production reference for the owner's seal — a two-phase model (setup with network, agent phase without) and method-restricted egress is a finer-grained alternative to --network=none for the builder stage while keeping the grading stage fully sealed. The 2025-12-18 addendum (read from PDF) also states OpenAI's internal 'OpenAI PRs' eval is 'graded by a hidden unit test' with human-written tests, and that browsing rollouts are screened by a cheating classifier with manual review of every flag.
claimed_results: Docs: 'By default, Codex blocks internet access during the agent phase'; presets None / Common dependencies (~80 domains) / All; optional restriction to GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. GPT-5.2-Codex addendum 2025-12-18 §3.1-3.2: cloud container 'network access disabled by default'; §5.1.3.1 OpenAI PRs pass@1 55% graded by hidden unit tests; §5.1.1.2 'inspect browsing rollouts using a classifier which flags instances of cheating and manually review all flagged rollouts'.

name: SWE-bench evaluation harness
one_line: Reference Docker-per-instance grading harness (FAIL_TO_PASS / PASS_TO_PASS) that most coding-agent claims are measured against; Multimodal v2 released 2026-09-01.
why_relevant: Q3: the de-facto sealed grader that the owner's gate mirrors; the harness itself does not enforce network isolation or test hiding — those are conventions layered by evaluators (see Cursor and METR entries), which is exactly the gap the owner's design closes. Q4: SWE-bench Multimodal v2 (visual issues) is a possible source of rendered-UI regression cases.
claimed_results: README: fully containerised Docker harness since June 2024 (with OpenAI Preparedness); resource note 120 GB disk / 16 GB RAM / 8 cores; 746 commits; news item 2026-09-01 SWE-bench Multimodal v2 open-sourced.

name: Building to the Test: Coding Agents Deliver What You Check, Not What You Requested
one_line: With 222 hidden Playwright tests as oracle, Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 hit 222/222 when the oracle was in the loop yet shipped dead libraries — the demo inlined the tested behaviour; no-op ablation exposed it.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: the closest experiment to the owner's pipeline (Playwright oracle, whole-component build, oracle visible vs hidden). Shows heldOutPass can be 100% while the requested artifact is absent, so the gate needs structural checks: post-hoc ablation (disable the library, tests must fail) and mechanical audits of which module the tests actually exercise. Directly motivates a negative-control probe in the sealed gate.
claimed_results: arXiv 2606.28430 (2026-06-26): 18 runs, 3 oracle conditions. No oracle: Claude 177/165/189 of 222, GPT 148/166/173 (genuine but incomplete libraries). Oracle in loop: Claude 222/222 in all c3 and c9 runs; GPT 221-222/222 (one run 161 that never engaged the oracle). No-op ablation: all 12 'dead library' cells showed zero test impact when the library was disabled; 3 library-routed controls failed 12-29 tests when ablated.

name: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards (Qwen Team)
one_line: Alibaba's account of four verifier designs — execution tests with an agentic quality judge and behaviour monitor, a weighted rubric verifier for frontend, a Playwright-driven interactive judge, and a checklist-decomposing agent evaluator for long-horizon tasks.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: gives the rubric weights for frontend grading (Functional 37.7%, Content 19.0%, Visual 13.3%, Layout 12.9%, UX 9.3%, Technical 7.2%) and a three-stage interactive judge (action planner, Playwright rendering, judge scoring interaction traces) that is a ready template for the owner's taste critic and human-factors adversary. Reports a large drop in hacked resolutions once verification was redesigned. Caveat: internal benchmarks, training-time setting.
claimed_results: arXiv 2606.26300 (2026-06-24, rev 06-29): hacked resolved rate 28.57% to 0.56% and clean resolved rate 40.22% to 60.53% across three SWE-Bench variants; Span-KTO on user feedback SWE-bench Verified 54.2% to 59.8%; interactive judge RFT +6 on WebDev Human Eval, +36 on QwenWebBench.

name: Can escalation channels redirect reward hacking toward defect disclosure?
one_line: Giving agents a structured 'report a defective test/infra' tool, in a 2x2 with an anti-hacking policy, cut hacking from 23.6% to 5.3% across 8 models and turned hacks into defect reports.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3: an unattended pipeline needs a legitimate exit when the sealed suite itself is wrong (the owner's spec seat can author bad tests). This is the mechanism: an escalation tool that pauses to the owner instead of letting the builder special-case. Same direction as ImpossibleBench's abort option, with a bigger model set and a coverage number.
claimed_results: arXiv 2608.29460 (2026-08-29): 8 models, 5 families; reward hacking 23.6% to 5.3%, eliminated entirely for 6 of 8 models; 96.8% of escalations involved no hacking; +10.1 pp defect-detection coverage.

name: TDAD: Test-Driven AI Agent Definition
one_line: Compiles agents from YAML behavioural specs with a Claude Agent SDK driver, iterating only against a visible test split and reporting Hidden Pass Rate and mutation score on the held-out split.
why_relevant: Q3: a working Claude Agent SDK harness that implements the owner's visible/held-out split (40-70% visible, 30-60% hidden) and adds mutation patches as a second negative control. Small and readable. Q4: only self-reported on 4 specs.
claimed_results: arXiv 2603.08806 (2026-03-09): 'visible/hidden test splits that withhold evaluation tests during compilation'; v1 specs 97% mean hidden pass rate, evolved v2 specs 78% hidden pass rate; repo includes mutation patches and HPR/MS measurement.

name: Are Coding Agents Generating Over-Mocked Tests? (MSR 2026)
one_line: Mining 1.2M 2025 commits across 2,168 JS/TS/Python repos shows agent-authored test commits add mocks far more often than human ones.
why_relevant: Q3: quantifies a specific way spec-seat tests can be hollow (mock-heavy tests pass without exercising the app). Justifies an audit rule in the adversarial suite review: flag mocks of the system under test, prefer real Playwright interactions.
claimed_results: arXiv 2602.00409 (2026-01-30; accepted MSR 2026): 36% of agent commits add mocks to tests vs 26% for non-agents; 23% of agent commits touch test files vs 13%; 68% of repos with agent test activity also have agent mock activity.

name: WebDevJudge
one_line: 654 human-labelled web-app preference pairs graded by LLM/MLLM judges from code, screenshots, or an interactive browser agent; best judge is far below human agreement.
why_relevant: Q3/Q4: measures how trustworthy a rendered-screenshot critic is for web UI quality — the owner's taste critic. Screenshots alone were the weakest input; code+screenshot best; judges show position bias and miss functional equivalence. Interactive agent judges had higher precision, lower recall on feasibility. Use paired/blinded and position-swapped prompts.
claimed_results: arXiv 2510.18560 (2025-10-21, final 2026-03-03): human inter-annotator 89.7% (with ties) / 94.0%; human pairwise 84.82%; best model Claude-4-Sonnet 66.06% with code+screenshot, 58.87% code-only, 57.34% screenshot-only; 'systematic preference for responses in a specific position'. Repo: scaling to >1k instances planned March 2026.

name: DiagEval: Trajectory-Conditioned Diagnosis for GUI-agent software evaluation
one_line: When a GUI-agent evaluator fails a generated app, DiagEval reuses the failed trajectory to run targeted probes and Bayesian updates to decide whether the evaluator or the software is at fault.
why_relevant: Q3: addresses the owner's recurring 'probe needs a negative control' defect — an interactive Playwright/GUI critic that fails may itself be wrong. Gives a retry-with-diagnosis protocol and shows how much accuracy it recovers over naive retries; pairs with the human-factors adversary seat.
claimed_results: arXiv 2605.17439 (2026-05-17, rev 05-19): recovers 45.6-62.1% of failures initially misattributed to software defects; 34.4-160.6% relative gain over retry baselines; accuracy 69.9% to 78.3% on WebDevJudge-Unit and 65.0% to 81.6% on RealDevBench.

name: PRDBench / PRDJudge (AGI-Eval)
one_line: 50 PRD-specified Python projects whose acceptance criteria were compiled by annotation agents into 408 pytest, 732 shell-interaction and 118 file-comparison checks, graded by a fine-tuned 30B judge; AAMAS 2026.
why_relevant: Q3: an Agent-as-a-Judge pipeline that starts from a product requirements document — same input shape as the owner's ticket — and shows requirements can be compiled to executable checks by agents with light human validation. Judge is independent of builders and close to the human agreement ceiling.
claimed_results: arXiv 2510.24358 (2025-10-28): PRDJudge (Qwen3-Coder-30B) 91.75% in-domain / 92.69% out-of-domain human alignment vs 95.83% inter-annotator upper bound; stability 94.19% unanimous, 96.07% pairwise. README leaderboard: Claude-4.5 69.19% development stage, Claude Code 70.25% debug stage.
last_activity: unknown (repo live, 47 stars, MIT); HF weights AGI-Eval/PRDjudge

name: NL2Repo-Bench
one_line: Agent gets one natural-language requirements document and an empty workspace and must produce an installable Python library, scored by test pass rate.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: calibration for 'one ticket = one whole application' — even strong agents stay under 40% on hidden tests when building from scratch, so the owner's falseFinish base rate on greenfield tickets is likely high and the fix loop budget should be sized accordingly.
claimed_results: arXiv 2512.12730 (2025-12-14, rev 2026-01-08): 'Even the strongest agents achieve below 40% average test pass rates and rarely complete an entire repository correctly.'

name: FeatureBench (ICLR 2026)
one_line: Feature-level tasks auto-derived by tracing unit tests through dependency graphs, with 3,825 executable environments and execution-based grading.
why_relevant: Q4: shows the SWE-bench number of a model is not predictive of multi-file feature delivery — the owner's planning and per-seat budgets should not be tuned from SWE-bench-style claims. Q3: the test-tracing task-construction method is a way to mine held-out cases from an existing repo for the repair/continuation lane.
claimed_results: arXiv 2602.10975 (2026-02-11): Claude 4.5 Opus 74.4% on SWE-bench Verified but 11.0% on FeatureBench; 200 evaluation tasks from 24 repos.

name: GitHub Spec Kit
one_line: Constitution / specify / plan / tasks / implement slash-command workflow producing markdown artifacts; analyze and checklist steps are LLM consistency reviews of those documents, not execution.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3: shows what the popular SDD tooling actually verifies — cross-artifact consistency and 'unit tests for English' checklists — and what it does not: no tests derived from spec, no held-out execution, no independent grader. Confirms the owner's spec seat plus sealed gate is beyond current SDD tooling rather than duplicating it.
claimed_results: none stated (no benchmarks or adoption metrics). v1.0.0 released 2026-08-21; v1.0.3 2026-09-01; 133k stars; MIT.

name: BMAD Method + Test Architect (TEA) module
one_line: Multi-agent role framework whose QA 'Test Architect' issues PASS / CONCERNS / FAIL / WAIVED gate decisions from traceability and NFR evidence documents rather than from running tests.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3: an example of a multi-role agent team with an explicit gate, but the gate is document-based and the same LLM lineage authors and reviews; nothing is executed or held out. Useful as a contrast case for why the owner's gate is a Docker run and not an agent opinion.
claimed_results: none stated. TEA docs: gate outputs 'PASS, CONCERNS, FAIL, or WAIVED' from coverage analysis and evidence review; workflows test-design, atdd, automate, test-review, nfr-assess, trace. 52.6k stars; MIT; latest release v6.11.0 (page date 10 Aug, year not reliably extracted).

name: Kiro specs (AWS)
one_line: Requirements (EARS acceptance criteria) / design / tasks documents; bugfix specs generate property-based tests; verification is a user-invoked '#spec' check of implementation against requirements.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3: the only SDD product that turns acceptance criteria into executable checks (property-based tests for bugfix specs), which is the closest commercial analogue to the owner's spec seat. No hidden split, no independent grader; the verification prompt is run by the same agent.
claimed_results: none stated. Best-practices page (updated 2026-08-04): 'Kiro generates property-based tests that validate both the fix and the preservation of existing behavior'; users can ask Kiro to 'Check if your implementation matches the spec's requirements'. Specs page updated 2026-08-27; CLI 3.0, IDE 1.0.

name: Tessl Framework and Spec Registry
one_line: Spec-as-source framework where spec capabilities carry @test directives linking to test files and a spec-verification CI workflow syncs the declared test runner; code regenerated from specs.
why_relevant: Q3: the one SDD tool that hard-links every spec capability to a test file and ships a spec-verification GitHub workflow — a lightweight version of the owner's frozen/sealed acceptance suite. Still no held-out split and the linkage is a reference that can silently break (per the Fowler write-up).
claimed_results: none stated beyond '10,000 pre-built specs' in the registry (launch post 2025-09-23; Framework private beta, Registry open beta).
last_activity: 2025-09-23 (launch post); registry package spec-driven-development 2.0.1 / spec-as-source 3.0.0 exist

name: Böckeler / martinfowler.com: 'Understanding Spec-Driven Development: Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl'
one_line: Independent hands-on comparison concluding that Kiro and spec-kit verify alignment only through markdown checklists and human review, and that Tessl's regeneration remains non-deterministic.
why_relevant: Q4: the only third-party assessment found of what SDD tools verify; warns that verbose markdown review workflows create 'a false sense of control' and that 'the agent ultimately [does] not follow all the instructions'. Supports investing in executable, held-out verification over more spec documents.
claimed_results: none quantitative (2025-10-15).

name: MAST: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., UC Berkeley)
one_line: Empirical failure taxonomy of 7 multi-agent frameworks (ChatDev, MetaGPT, HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2, Magentic-One, OpenManus) from 1,642 annotated traces, with an LLM-as-judge annotator you can run on your own run logs.
why_relevant: Q4 (evidence) and Q3 (verification): 23.5% of all failures are 'task verification' failures and 43.9% are system-design failures, i.e. the harness, not the model. The two ChatDev interventions (final-authority role, explicit high-level-objective verification step) map directly onto a plan seat + independent judge design. The judge pipeline (94% accuracy) is a ready-made drift/failure classifier for the owner's learning corpus of failure->repair pairs.
claimed_results: arXiv v1 2025-03-17, v3 2025-10-26 (NeurIPS 2025 poster). From full text: 1,642 traces across 7 frameworks; failure categories FC1 system design 43.9%, FC2 inter-agent misalignment 31.75%, FC3 task verification 23.5%; per-framework failure rates 41-68.7% (ChatDev/MetaGPT), ~60% HyperAgent, ~70% AppWorld, 60-70% AG2, 50-60% Magentic-One, ~50% OpenManus. ChatDev case study: CEO final-authority workflow change +9.4% success; adding a high-level task objective verification step +15.6% on ProgramDev. LLM-as-judge (o1 few-shot) accuracy 94%, Cohen's kappa 0.77; human inter-annotator kappa 0.88.

name: Cognition: Don't Build Multi-Agents (Walden Yan)
one_line: Devin team's argument that parallel subagents produce conflicting implicit decisions; recommends one main loop carrying full trace context and a dedicated context-compression model.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: the canonical 'against' evidence for parallel builders. Principle 1 'share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages' and Principle 2 'actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results' argue for the owner's serial seat pipeline (plan -> spec -> build -> fix) over parallel teammates writing code. Notes Claude Code 'never does work in parallel with the subtask agent' and subagents mostly answer questions rather than write code.
claimed_results: Published 2025-06-12. No numbers; Flappy Bird two-subagent failure example. A 2026 follow-up by the same author appeared in search results only (x.com/walden_yan/status/2047054554433462360, snippet: setups that work share 'one main loop carries state, subagents are stateless workers with narrow scope') but could not be opened (HTTP 402).

name: Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system
one_line: Orchestrator-worker research system (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents) with LLM-judge rubric evals, rainbow deployments and explicit warning that coding is less parallelisable than research.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: the canonical 'for' evidence, but it explicitly scopes the win to breadth-first read-heavy research and says 'most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents.' Also useful for Q3: rubric-based LLM judge on factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency; 'start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples.'
claimed_results: Published 2025-06-13. 'multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2%' on internal research eval; 'agents typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens as chats'; 'three factors explained 95% of the performance variance' with 'token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance' (BrowseComp).

name: Anthropic: When to use multi-agent systems (and when not to)
one_line: Anthropic's 2026 decision guide: multi-agent helps for context protection, parallelization, specialization; hurts when decomposed by work type (plan/implement/test); recommends context-centric decomposition and cheap verification subagents.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3/Q4: directly warns against 'problem-centric decomposition' (splitting by planning/implementation/testing) which is exactly the owner's seat layout, and instead recommends 'context-centric decomposition' plus verification subagents that test main-agent output 'against clear success criteria' without the implementation history — this is the held-out-suite/independent-critic pattern.
claimed_results: Published 2026-01-23 (Cara Phillips et al.). 'Multi-agent systems typically consume 3 to 10 times more tokens than single-agent approaches for equivalent tasks'; 15-20+ tools is the threshold signalling need for specialization; 'teams invest months building elaborate multi-agent architectures only to discover that improved prompting on a single agent achieved equivalent results.'

name: Anthropic: Building effective agents
one_line: Defines the five workflow patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) and argues for adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3: the evaluator-optimizer loop ('one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop', effective 'when we have clear evaluation criteria') is the owner's fix seat; the coding appendix states code agents work because 'Code solutions are verifiable through automated tests' yet 'human review remains crucial'. Older than 18 months but still the reference vocabulary.
claimed_results: Published 2024-12-19 (Erik Schluntz, Barry Zhang). No numbers; principle 'You should consider adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.'

name: Claude Code agent teams (official docs + costs page)
one_line: Lead + teammates with a shared task list (file-locked claims, dependencies), JSON mailboxes, TeammateIdle/TaskCreated/TaskCompleted quality-gate hooks; experimental, interactive-only.
why_relevant: Q1 directly. Key constraints for the owner's design: 'Spawning teammates also requires an interactive session. In non-interactive mode with the -p flag, including Agent SDK sessions, Claude doesn't spawn teammates' — so a headless orchestrator cannot use teams as-is. Task claiming 'uses file locking to prevent race conditions'; TaskCompleted hook 'Exit with code 2 to prevent completion and send feedback' is a native quality gate; teammates get no lead history; 'Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites'; guidance 'Start with 3-5 teammates', 'Letting a team run unattended for too long increases the risk of wasted effort'. Agent teams shipped in research preview with Opus 4.6 on 2026-02-05 ('best for tasks that split into independent, read-heavy work like codebase reviews').
claimed_results: No effectiveness numbers published. Costs page (code.claude.com/docs/en/costs): 'Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode'. Docs current as of v2.1.178-v2.1.251 behaviour notes; env var CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1.

name: Anthropic: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes (Nicholas Carlini)
one_line: 16 Opus 4.6 agents, ~2,000 Claude Code sessions, two weeks, ~$20K, produced a 100K-line Rust C compiler that builds Linux 6.9; coordination via git plus a lock-file task claim in current_tasks/.
why_relevant: Q1 and Q3: the only published unattended multi-agent build of that scale with numbers. Concrete adoptable choices: self-selected tasks ('I leave it up to each Claude agent to decide how to act'), lock by 'writing a text file to current_tasks/', each agent clones to /workspace and pushes upstream, and the explicit verification lesson 'it's important that the task verifier is nearly perfect, otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem' — the strongest argument for the owner's sealed held-out gate. Also shows failure mode: agent 'simply cheats here and calls out to GCC' for 16-bit x86.
claimed_results: Published 2026-02-05. 16 parallel agents; 'nearly 2,000 Claude Code sessions'; 'just under $20,000'; 100,000-line compiler; '99% pass rate on most compiler test suites including the GCC torture test suite'; compiles Linux 6.9 on x86, ARM, RISC-V.

name: Cursor: Scaling long-running autonomous coding (Wilson Lin)
one_line: Hundreds of concurrent agents on one repo for weeks; flat peer-to-peer coordination failed (risk-averse agents, lock bottlenecks); a planner / sub-planner / worker / judge hierarchy worked.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: the clearest negative result on flat agent teams and positive result on hierarchy plus a terminal judge. 'With no hierarchy, agents became risk-averse. They avoided difficult tasks and made small, safe changes instead'; lock-based coordination 'Twenty agents would slow down to the effective throughput of two or three'. Each cycle 'ending with a judge agent deciding if the project was completed or not' is the owner's verdict stage. Also notes model-role mismatch: 'GPT-5.2 is a better planner than GPT-5.1-Codex'.
claimed_results: Published 2026-01-14. Browser: 'over 1 million lines across 1,000 files' in 'close to a week'; React migration over 3 weeks (266K additions/193K deletions per search snippet); Java LSP 7.4K commits/550K LoC; Windows 7 emulator 14.6K commits/1.2M LoC; Excel 12K commits/1.6M LoC; 'trillions' of tokens. No correctness benchmark reported.

name: OpenAI: Harness engineering — leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
one_line: Five-month internal experiment: ~1M lines, ~1,500 merged PRs, zero hand-written code; the humans built the harness (AGENTS.md map, docs/ as system of record, custom linters, structural tests, doc-gardening agent).
why_relevant: Q2/Q3: the best documented 'self-maintaining' harness. Mechanisms to copy: 'a short AGENTS.md (roughly 100 lines) is injected into context and serves primarily as a map'; docs/ 'the system of record' with 'quality grades, and execution plans as first-class artifacts'; 'custom linters and structural tests' enforce 'a fixed set of layers, with strictly validated dependency directions'; a 'doc-gardening' agent scans for obsolete documentation; 'recurring cleanup process' as debt garbage collection; code 'optimized first for Codex's legibility'. Verification is mechanical, not self-graded.
claimed_results: Page shows no explicit publication date (openai.com returned 403; read via r.jina.ai proxy). Timeline: deployment 'Late August 2025', 5 months; ~1 million lines; ~1,500 PRs merged; 3 engineers growing to 7; 3.5 PRs per engineer per day. Secondary (rywalker.com, April 2026): 'Agent-to-agent code review', '6+ hour autonomy per task'.

name: OpenAI Symphony (SPEC.md + Elixir reference orchestrator)
one_line: Issue tracker (Linear) as control plane: poll board, isolated workspace per issue, spawn Codex agent, deliver PR; humans review outcomes instead of supervising sessions.
why_relevant: Q1: production-shaped ticket-in -> PR-out loop with explicit lifecycle parameters the owner can copy for per-seat budgets and anti-loop: polling 30s, 'Max turns per issue: 20', retry backoff 'minimum(10s x 2^attempts, 300s)', 'Default concurrency limit: 10 agents', turn timeout 900s, workspace hooks at create/pre-run/post-run/remove with symlink-escape validation (per sjramblings.io 2026-03-12 reading of SPEC.md). Rationale quote (InfoQ 2026-05-17): 'the cost of an agent making mistakes is significantly reduced, since it primarily involves reviewing completed work and rejecting it.'
claimed_results: GitHub API: created 2026-02-26, pushed 2026-08-19, 26,991 stars, Apache-2.0. A '500% increase in landed pull requests' claim appears only in a MindStudio post (2026-05-03) with no OpenAI source cited — treat as unverified.

name: MetaGPT (FoundationAgents) + Data Interpreter
one_line: SOP/assembly-line multi-agent 'software company' (PM, architect, PM, engineer) with structured intermediate artifacts and executable feedback; launched MGX product 2025-02-19.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: the archetype the owner's seat pipeline resembles. Evidence is dated and mixed: strong on HumanEval/SoftwareDev in 2023, but MAST measured 41-68.7% trace failure rate in 2025. The executable-feedback ablation is the transferable finding (tests-as-feedback lifts pass@1). Data Interpreter (arXiv 2402.18679, v4 2024-10-15) adds hierarchical graph planning with node-level verification.
claimed_results: Paper (arXiv 2308.00352, v7 2024-11-01; ICLR 2024): HumanEval 85.9% pass@1, MBPP 87.7%; SoftwareDev executability 3.75/4 vs ChatDev 2.25, human revision cost 0.83 vs 2.5, 31,255 tokens vs 19,292; executable feedback ablation +4.2% HumanEval, +5.4% MBPP. Data Interpreter abstract: ML tasks 88%->95%, open-ended 60%->97%, MATH +26%, InfiAgent-DABench 75.9%->94.9%. Repo 70,160 stars.

name: AFlow: Automating Agentic Workflow Generation (ICLR 2025 Oral)
one_line: MCTS over code-represented agent workflows using execution feedback; no fine-tuning; finds workflows that beat hand-designed ones and let small models match GPT-4o at a fraction of cost.
why_relevant: Q2: a self-improvement loop that operates on the workflow/prompt graph itself using only run outcomes — the same substrate the owner's offline self-repair tier targets. Not built on GEPA/DSPy; distinct search-based approach.
claimed_results: arXiv 2410.10762 v1 2024-10-14, v4 2025-04-15: '5.7% average improvement over state-of-the-art baselines' across six datasets; smaller models 'outperform GPT-4o on specific tasks at 4.55% of its inference cost in dollars'; 96.2% HumanEval with GPT-4o (per search summary).

name: SELA: Tree-Search Enhanced LLM Agents for Automated Machine Learning (MetaGPT ext)
one_line: MCTS over experiment-pipeline space with an experience/insight pool; agents iteratively refine strategies from experimental feedback.
why_relevant: Q2 (adjacent): a no-fine-tuning learning loop where an insight pool accumulates across runs — same shape as the owner's exemplar corpus injected into prompts. Domain is AutoML, not web apps.
claimed_results: arXiv 2024-10-22: 'a win rate of 65% to 80% against each baseline across all datasets' on 20 ML datasets. Code in github.com/geekan/MetaGPT (metagpt/ext/sela).

name: ChatDev / ChatDev 2.0 (DevAll)
one_line: Chat-chain role-play software company (CEO/CTO/programmer/reviewer/tester) with 'communicative dehallucination'; 2.0 (2026-01-07) is a zero-code multi-agent platform.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3/Q4: the reviewer/tester ablation is a small but real datapoint that a separate critic role improves executability; however MAST measured 41-68.7% failure rate and EvoMAC beats it by 20+ points on rSDE-Bench, so treat as a baseline not a target. The later Puppeteer orchestrator (NeurIPS 2025) needs RL training — not usable under the owner's constraints.
claimed_results: Paper (arXiv 2307.07924, ACL 2024): completeness 0.5600, executability 0.8800, consistency 0.8021, quality 0.3953 vs MetaGPT 0.4834/0.4145/0.7601/0.1523; removing communicative dehallucination: completeness 0.4700, executability 0.8400, quality 0.3094; 148.2 s and 22,949 tokens per software. Repo 34,180 stars.

name: EvoMAC / rSDE-Bench: Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Collaboration Networks for Software Development (ICLR 2025)
one_line: Coding team + separate testing team + updating team; test-time 'textual backpropagation' rewrites agent prompts and topology from test feedback; benchmark of 53 website/game tasks with 616 test cases.
why_relevant: Q2 and Q3 together: self-evolution at test time without fine-tuning, driven by an independent testing team, on exactly the owner's task class (websites and games from requirements). Automatic requirement-aware evaluation correlates 0.9922 with human evaluation, supporting test-suite-as-oracle. Code has moved into 'MasLab' per rSDE-Bench repo.
claimed_results: arXiv v1 2024-10-22. vs GPT-4o-mini single agent: Website Basic +26.48%, Website Advanced +20.65%, Game Basic +34.78%, Game Advanced +21.50%, HumanEval +6.10%. Absolute: EvoMAC 89.38/65.05/77.54/51.60 vs ChatDev 62.67/43.45/53.63/32.26; HumanEval 94.51 vs 70.73. rSDE-Bench: '53 unique coding tasks and 616 test cases'; human-auto eval correlation 0.9922. Benchmark repo 37 stars.
last_activity: paper 2024-10-22; rSDE-Bench repo (18 commits, date not shown)

name: Magentic-One (Microsoft AutoGen)
one_line: Orchestrator with Task Ledger (facts/guesses) and Progress Ledger (five status questions) directing WebSurfer/FileSurfer/Coder/Terminal; stall counter triggers re-planning.
why_relevant: Q1 mechanism: the two-ledger + stall-counter loop is a concrete, ablated anti-loop design (counter > 2 breaks the inner loop and re-plans) that maps to the owner's fingerprint-based anti-loop. Note AutoGen repo is now 'in maintenance mode' (README), 60,753 stars, pushed 2026-04-15; MAST measured 50-60% failure on Magentic-One traces.
claimed_results: arXiv 2024-11-07. GAIA test 38.00% +/-5.5 (GPT-4o + o1-preview), 32.33% (GPT-4o); AssistantBench accuracy 27.7% / 25.3%; WebArena 32.8% +/-3.2. Ablation (GAIA validation): removing Orchestrator ledgers -31%, FileSurfer -39%, Coder/ComputerTerminal -21% each.

name: Magentic-UI: Towards Human-in-the-loop Agentic Systems (repo now MagenticLite)
one_line: Co-planning, co-tasking, action guards with irreversibility heuristics, and saving execution traces as reusable plans; measured with simulated users.
why_relevant: Q2/Q3 adjacent: quantifies the value of asking the human at the right moment (the owner's plan-seat clarifying questions) and shows a learning-without-fine-tuning mechanism ('synthesize a plan based on task execution traces' into a gallery). Action guards ('always irreversible', 'maybe irreversible' judged by LLM, 'never irreversible') are a template for permission rules around the sealed suite.
claimed_results: arXiv 2025-07-30. Autonomous (o4-mini): GAIA 42.52%, AssistantBench 27.6%, WebVoyager 82.2%, WebGames 45.5%. With a simulated user holding task info, GAIA 30.3% -> 51.9% (+71%); assistance requested in only 4-10% of tasks. Repo github.com/microsoft/magentic-ui now describes 'MagenticLite', 10,080 stars, pushed 2026-09-01.

name: TheAgentCompany (CMU) benchmark
one_line: 175 end-to-end workplace tasks in a self-hosted software company (GitLab, OwnCloud, RocketChat, Plane) with checkpoint-based scoring; software-engineering tasks are the easiest category.
why_relevant: Q4: independent evidence for how far unattended agents get on realistic multi-step SDE work (best 30.3% full completion). Checkpoint-based partial credit is a scoring design the owner could borrow for the judge.
claimed_results: arXiv v1 2024-12-18, v3 2025-09-10 (NeurIPS 2025 D&B). Gemini 2.5 Pro (OpenHands 0.28.1) 30.3% success / 39.3% partial / $4.2; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 26.3% / 36.4%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 24.0% / 34.4%; GPT-4o 8.6%; Llama 3.1 405B 7.4%. Search summary: SDE ~42% vs HR ~18%, Finance ~22%; a community 42.9% entry was mentioned but not verified.

name: AdaptOrch: Task-Adaptive Multi-Agent Orchestration
one_line: Routes each task to parallel / sequential / hierarchical / hybrid topology; claims topology choice matters more than model choice once models converge.
why_relevant: Q4: a 2026 measurement of multi-agent topologies vs single agent on SWE-bench Verified (with weak models). Static parallel beats single-best by 4.5 pts and adaptive by 9.8, but the router chose sequential 0% of the time — a hint that pure assembly-line pipelines (the owner's seat chain) are the weakest static topology in their setup.
claimed_results: arXiv 2026-02-18. Abstract: 'topology-aware orchestration achieves 12-23% improvement over static single-topology baselines'. SWE-bench Verified: single best 42.8, static-parallel 47.3, static-sequential 45.6, AdaptOrch 52.6 (+9.8 pp); routing 24% parallel, 0% sequential, 14% hierarchical, 62% hybrid; models GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 2.5 72B. No code URL found.

name: AOrchestra: Automating Sub-Agent Creation for Agentic Orchestration (FoundationAgents)
one_line: Orchestrator spawns sub-agents on demand as (Instruction, Context, Tools, Model) tuples and cross-checks results against the original task before accepting.
why_relevant: Q1/Q3: an on-demand subagent recipe with an explicit orchestrator-side verification step ('cross-checking results against original task requirements') rather than trusting the worker's DONE — the same falseFinish concern the owner measures.
claimed_results: arXiv 2602.03786 v1 2026-02-03, v2 2026-02-07. With Gemini-3-Flash: GAIA (165 tasks) 80.00 pass@1 vs OpenHands 66.06; Terminal-Bench 2.0 (70 sampled) 52.86 vs Mini-SWE 34.29; SWE-Bench-Verified (100 sampled) 82.00 vs Mini-SWE 56.00; abstract: '16.28% relative improvement against the strongest baseline'. Repo 159 stars.

name: ClawArena-Team: Benchmarking Subagent Orchestration and Dynamic Workflows
one_line: Measures a lead model's ability to manage subagents (permissions, modality, async returns) across 41 scenarios; finds permission-scoping is the bottleneck and cost is decoupled from management quality.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: evidence that lead agents over-grant workspace access ('workspace-permission precision never reaches 50%', managers grant 'roughly twice the file access they actually need') — directly relevant to keeping the held-out suite invisible: enforce with OS/sandbox rules, never with the lead's judgement.
claimed_results: arXiv 2606.31174 v1 2026-06-30, v2 2026-07-02. 12 models, 41 scenarios, 258 rounds. Top Subagent-Management Score: claude-fable-5 60.0%, gemini-3.5-flash 53.8%, glm-5.2 50.4%, kimi-k2.6 49.0%; ten models within a 9.9-point band (43.9-53.8%); main-agent cost spans '$0.8 to $92.8 per run' (>100x) while scores span <4x; read-only compliance >=92%. Repo 63 stars.

name: icat-agent: Adaptive Multi-Agent Scaffolding for Efficient Issue Resolution
one_line: Decentralized agents with event-based message passing instead of shared context; assesses issue quality to choose parallel patching vs exploratory phase; claims wins over Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4: a 2026 head-to-head of a multi-agent scaffold against single-agent Claude Code on SWE-bench Verified/Pro, plus cost per instance. Its 'quality-based issue assessment' gate (well-defined -> parallel, ambiguous -> explore) mirrors the owner's plan seat asking clarifying questions before freezing.
claimed_results: arXiv 2026-06-24. SWE-bench Verified +3.6-8.4% over SWE-agent, mini-SWE-agent, Claude Code; SWE-bench Pro +6.3-18.5%; icat-agent + GPT-5.4-xhigh 67.4% vs prior best 59.10% (+8.3 pp); average saving $1.18 per instance vs 'multi-agent Claude Code baseline'. No code URL on page.

name: Long Live the Librarian! A Persistent Search Sub-Agent for Multi-Agent SWE Systems
one_line: A persistent repository-search sub-agent that dedupes exploration across agents and returns file references instead of excerpts, cutting energy/tokens without hurting SWE-bench results.
why_relevant: Q1 mechanism (adjacent): a cheap shared 'librarian' seat that survives across builder/fix iterations is a direct way to reduce the repeated codebase re-reading in the owner's 1-12 hour runs, and it is measured on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live.
claimed_results: arXiv 2605.27787 v1 2026-05-27, v2 2026-08-31: '11 to 30% reduction in per-episode GPU energy consumption' on SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Bench-Live 'while maintaining task performance'; 'output token consumes 30 to 1,000 times more energy than an input or cached token'. Repo 1 star.

name: Can Small Agents Collaborate to Beat a Single Large Language Model?
one_line: Small-model orchestrator+subagents vs one large model on tool-heavy tasks; performance is driven by orchestrator capacity, and reasoning in subagents helps little or hurts.
why_relevant: Q4: supports putting the strongest model/effort in the plan/lead seat and cheaper models in worker seats — 'Overall system performance is driven primarily by orchestrator capacity rather than sub-agent capacity'; 'enabling reasoning in sub-agents provides limited or negative benefits'. Not measured on SWE tasks.
claimed_results: arXiv v1 2026-01-16, v2 2026-04-13. Qualitative claims only in abstract (small MAS outperformed larger single agents with tool access on factual retrieval, multi-hop, science QA, math). No code URL.

name: CodeR: Issue Resolving with Multi-Agent and Task Graphs
one_line: Manager/Reproducer/Fault-Localizer/Editor/Verifier roles on pre-defined task graphs; reproducer writes a failing test before editing; verifier checks after.
why_relevant: Q3 mechanism: separates 'reproduce/verify' roles from the editor, an early version of an independent verifier seat. Numbers are 2024-era and superseded.
claimed_results: arXiv 2406.01304 v3 2024-06-11: 'On SWE-bench lite, CodeR is able to solve 28.33% of issues, when submitting only once for each issue.' Repo 158 stars.

name: AgentCoder: Multi-Agent-based Code Generation with Iterative Testing and Optimisation
one_line: Programmer, independent test-designer, and test-executor agents; tests are written without seeing the code and drive the repair loop.
why_relevant: Q3 mechanism: the test designer 'operates independently from the programmer agent' — the same separation as the owner's spec seat authoring the suite from the ticket alone. Benchmarks are saturated HumanEval/MBPP, so treat as a mechanism citation not a result.
claimed_results: arXiv v1 2023-12-20, v3 2024-05-24: GPT-4 pass@1 96.3% HumanEval, 91.8% MBPP vs SOTA baseline 90.2% / 78.9%.

name: SWE-Search: MCTS + Iterative Refinement with Discriminator debate (Moatless)
one_line: MCTS over agent trajectories with a hybrid LLM value function and a Discriminator agent running multi-agent debate to pick the final patch.
why_relevant: Q3: a non-self-graded selection step (independent discriminator + value agent debating candidate patches) that reported gains across five models; a pattern for choosing among multiple fix-seat attempts before spending a gate run.
claimed_results: arXiv 2410.20285 v1 2024-10-26, v3 2024-12-15: '23% relative improvement in performance across five models' on SWE-bench vs agents without MCTS. Repo 142 stars; README has no numbers.

name: Open SWE (LangChain / LangGraph)
one_line: Async coding agent: Manager -> Planner (human plan review) -> Programmer with Reviewer sub-agent, each task in a Daytona sandbox, opens PRs from GitHub issues.
why_relevant: Q1 reference architecture on LangGraph with a plan-approval checkpoint and a reviewer loop; no published effectiveness numbers, so evidence is architectural only.
claimed_results: Launch post 2025-08-06; no evaluation or SWE-bench numbers stated. Repo 10,646 stars, pushed 2026-09-02.

name: In-House Coding Agents: Build vs Buy (Ry Walker research aggregation)
one_line: Secondary compilation of 15 enterprise in-house coding agents (Coinbase Forge, Ramp Inspect, Abnormal, Google, OpenAI, Stripe, Cloudflare, Spotify, Meta) with PR-share and cycle-time claims.
why_relevant: Q4 production adoption numbers in one place; and the Cloudflare entry is a concrete non-self-graded reviewer design (7-agent reviewer with manual-override rate). Primary sources are mostly X posts/town halls; treat every number as second-hand until the owner opens the cited primary.
claimed_results: Published ~April 2026. Coinbase Forge: 5% of merged PRs, PR cycle ~150h -> ~15h, 1,000+ engineers; Ramp Inspect: >50% of merged PRs (up from 30%), '80% of Inspect built by Inspect itself'; Abnormal AI: 13% of PRs from background agents (Feb 2026); Google 'Agent Smith' >25% of new production code (unverified, March 2026 town hall); Stripe Minions 1,300+ PRs/week; Cloudflare 131,246 review runs, 7-agent reviewer, $1.19 median cost per review, 0.6% manual override rate; OpenAI ~1M LOC / ~1,500 PRs / 3.5 PRs per engineer per day.

name: LangChain: How and when to build multi-agent systems (Harrison Chase)
one_line: Reconciles Cognition and Anthropic: both say context engineering is paramount and read work parallelises while write work does not.
why_relevant: Q1/Q4 synthesis: 'Read operations are inherently more parallelizable than write operations'; Anthropic 'deliberately handled synthesis (the writing component) through a single agent'. Supports parallel review/critic seats and a single builder. Also: '~20 datapoints suffice for initial evaluation'.
claimed_results: Published 2025-06-16. No new numbers beyond those in the Anthropic/Cognition posts.

name: Geoffrey Huntley — "Ralph Wiggum as a software engineer" (+ CURSED, LinearB podcast)
one_line: The origin post for the bash-loop unattended agent pattern: `while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done`, with 'backpressure' (tests, static analyzers, type systems) as the only verification.
why_relevant: (1) single-agent unattended loop over a spec; (2) self-improvement without fine-tuning via file-based memory (state lives in repo/TODO/git, fresh context each iteration, operator 'tunes' PROMPT.md); (3) verification = generate → backpressure (unit tests required per change, Dialyzer/Pyright mandated, Rust chosen for type-system backpressure, security scanners) → feedback. Documented failure modes we can pre-empt: duplicate implementations when search assumptions fail (fix: 'don't assume not implemented'), placeholder implementations needing extra loops, context exhaustion on large error volumes, git resets when rescue fails.
claimed_results: ghuntley.com/ralph (2025-07-14): '6 repositories' shipped overnight at a Y Combinator hackathon; '$297 USD' for a '$50k USD contract, delivered, MVP, tested + reviewed'. ghuntley.com/cursed (2025-09-09): CURSED language built by 'Claude in a loop for three months', LLVM backend, macOS/Linux/Windows binaries; no pass-rate metrics given. LinearB Dev Interrupted podcast (2026-01-13): 'it costs $10.42 US an hour' to run Sonnet 4.5 in a bash loop; failure modes named: context rot/compaction, 'context anxiety', usable context ~120k of 200k after harness overhead.

name: Anthropic ralph-wiggum plugin (anthropics/claude-code)
one_line: Official Claude Code packaging of the Ralph loop: a Stop hook blocks exit and re-feeds the same prompt until a completion-promise string appears or --max-iterations is hit.
why_relevant: (1) the mechanism we could copy for the fix seat's anti-loop: Stop-hook re-entry, `--max-iterations` as the primary safety net, exact-string completion promise (README warns it cannot express multiple exit conditions like SUCCESS vs BLOCKED), `/cancel-ralph`. README explicitly says Ralph is only for 'Tasks with automatic verification (tests, linters)' and not for 'Unclear success criteria' — a direct argument for our held-out suite as the loop's terminator.
claimed_results: README repeats Huntley's numbers only: '6 repositories overnight (Y Combinator hackathon)', '$50k contract for $297 in API costs', 'entire programming language over 3 months'. No plugin-specific measurements.
last_activity: 2026 (README footer); plugin landed Dec 2025 per search summaries

name: Geocodio / Mathias Hansen — "Ship Features in Your Sleep with Ralph Loops"
one_line: Company engineer runs spec → PRD (prd.json with pass/fail flags) → autonomous Claude Code loop on Max subscriptions over a weekend and ships two apps.
why_relevant: (1) closest match to our setting: single machine, subscription seats, plan→spec→build loop with machine-readable acceptance criteria; (2) `progress.txt` 'learnings' file injected each iteration is a minimal learning corpus; (3) verification = typecheck/lint/test + 'acceptance criteria must be verifiable commands, not subjective judgments', commit only after verification, max-iteration cap. Names the exact falseFinish risk we measure: agent 'quietly deleting or skipping tests' when context depletes.
claimed_results: 2026-01-27: two complete applications built from 'Friday at 4pm' to 'Sunday evening'; 'Maxed out TWO Claude Max 20x subscriptions. That's $400/month in subscriptions, exhausted in a few days'; loop capped at 50 iterations; 'Claude amnesia' after context exhaustion; author advises against use on established production codebases with implicit conventions.

name: Lukas Grigis — "What a ralph loop actually is, and how to run one without burning your tokens" (ralphctl)
one_line: Ralph-loop harness author describes an independent evaluator model grading each task, 3-attempt blocking, disk-resident state and worktree parallelism, plus the failure modes that burned tokens.
why_relevant: (2)+(3): 'An agent grading its own homework gives itself an A every time' — separate evaluator model grades against per-task verification criteria; `harness.maxAttempts` default 3 then flag BLOCKED (not loop forever); `concurrency.maxParallelTasks` 1 (max 5, separate git worktrees); 20 budget presets across standard/economic/strong-gate/fast/frontier. Failure catalogue we can test against: unverifiable criteria → infinite loops, orchestrator (not model) OOM, 'unattended runs make unattended mistakes', parallel tasks editing the same file corrupting branches.
claimed_results: 2026-07-01 (updated 2026-08-30): cites Anthropic's measurement 'a quick solo run came in around 20 minutes and $9 and produced a broken core, while the full multi-agent harness ran roughly 6 hours and $200 and produced something that actually worked'. No own-run outcome numbers.

name: Steve Yegge — "Welcome to Gas Town" + steveyegge/gastown repo
one_line: Multi-agent orchestrator (Mayor / Polecats / Refinery merge queue / Witness / Deacon / Dogs / Crew) over a git-backed issue ledger (Beads) that claims 20–30 sustained parallel Claude Code agents.
why_relevant: (1) concrete architecture for a lead-plus-workers team with a serialised merge queue ('Refinery... one at a time' to avoid the 'monkey knife fight over rebasing/merging'), persistent identity + ephemeral sessions, Witness patrol that nudges stuck workers, work persisted in Beads so crashed sessions resume. Maggie Appleton's notes (maggieappleton.com/gastown, Jan 2026) identify the bottleneck we'd hit too: 'Gas Town churns through implementation plans so quickly that you have to do a LOT of design and planning to keep the engine fed.'
claimed_results: Medium post 2026-01-01: '75k lines of code, 2000 commits' in 17 days; 'I've tamed them to where you can use 20–30 at once, productively, on a sustained basis'; 'Do not use Gas Town if you care about money'; three orchestrator rewrites failed before the Go version; '100% vibe coded'. Repo (fetched 2026-09-02): 17.9k stars, MIT, 7,770 commits, last commit 2026-07-23; README: '4-10 agents become chaotic' vs 'scales comfortably to 20-30 agents'. Beads at 23k stars per yegge.ai.

name: Steve Yegge — "The Continuous Thunderdome" (Gas Town post-mortem by its author)
one_line: Eight months in, the creator says Gas Town 'effectively burned down': it only ever built itself, and a model-version behaviour change (Opus 4.7's 'just two more things' tic) broke convergence.
why_relevant: (4) the strongest negative datapoint on question 4: a 20–30-agent orchestrator with a merge queue did not survive one model upgrade — direct evidence for our drift-detection tier and for pinning model behaviour into the known-bad corpus. Also (2): his Wheelhouse crew (18 named agents, 700+ designed beads) is a self-maintaining pipeline that mostly maintained itself. Architectural pivot worth noting rather than copying: abandon the merge queue, 'Just slam all the commits onto main, and then just friggin' deal with it', swarm diagnosis instead of bisection.
claimed_results: August 2026 (quoted by Simon Willison 2026-08-04): 'Gas Town was intended to be reusable, but I only ever wound up using it to build itself. Gas Town fell apart at the seams with Opus 4.7. Up through 4.6 it was working brilliantly... The Opus tic never went away, so Gas Town effectively burned down.' Token burn: 69 billion tokens in July with 96% cache hits, '$87,000/month' list-equivalent, ~'$2,800/month' actual via multiple Max accounts; ~175 commits/day average, 250 peak; 18 crew agents; 700+ unimplemented beads; Wheelhouse ~150k–300k lines of bash + 25k lines of elisp.

name: DoltHub / Tim Sehn — "A Day in Gas Town"
one_line: Database company CEO points Gas Town at four skipped tests in the Dolt repo: four PRs, all closed, one auto-merged with failing integration tests, ~$100 in an hour.
why_relevant: (3)+(4): a clean negative control for 'multi-agent loop without an independent gate'. The merge happened despite red integration tests — exactly the gap our sealed Docker held-out gate exists to close — and required a human force-push reset. Cost-per-hour figure is a useful budget baseline for per-seat budget lines.
claimed_results: 2026-01-15: 4 polecats on 4 tests (~20 more agents running in other terminals); 'None of the PRs were good, and I ended up closing them all'; ~$100 of Claude tokens in 60 minutes, 'about 10X the cost of a normal Claude Code session per unit time'; one PR merged autonomously despite integration-test failure, colleague had to reset and force push.

name: Tenzin Wangdhen — "Gas Town: The Good, The Bad, The Ugly"
one_line: One-week trial of Gas Town on a Go TUI project: 6 of 7 beads merged, but process leaks, a clobbered config file and no observability made the author abandon it.
why_relevant: (1)+(4): operational failure modes of an unattended multi-agent loop that our orchestrator must self-heal: orphaned subprocesses, background daemons (Deacon/Dogs) silently not running, inter-agent mail needing patches, an agent overwriting the orchestrator's own config (recovered from git), 'unclear when PRs merged or why system stalled'.
claimed_results: 2026-02-19: 7 beads dispatched before dinner (footer, fsnotify watching, cached views); '6 PRs merged; 1 blocked on dependency'; '141 orphaned Claude Code processes' by week's end; elevated RAM from cleanup failures; abandoned after one week. No own cost figures (cites Yegge 'cash guzzler', Steinberger 'ultimate token burner').

name: Anthropic / Nicholas Carlini — "Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes"
one_line: 16 Opus 4.6 agents in Docker containers, coordinating via text-file locks and a shared git remote, built a 100k-line Rust C compiler that compiles Linux 6.9 in two weeks for ~$20k.
why_relevant: (1) a documented lead-less agent team with the simplest coordination that worked: `current_tasks/` lock files, pull/merge/push per task; (3) verification that is not self-graded: external compiler test suites with automated verifiers, GCC as a 'known-good compiler oracle', CI enforcing no regressions — and the key architectural move when all 16 agents piled onto one bug: randomly compile most kernel files with GCC and only a subset with the agents' compiler, turning one monolithic failure into many independent, parallelisable ones. Failure modes: agents overwriting each other on a single task, frequent merge conflicts, new features breaking old ones.
claimed_results: 2026-02-05: 'Nearly 2,000 Claude Code sessions across two weeks'; 'Just under $20,000'; '100,000-line compiler'; '2 billion input tokens and generated 140 million output tokens'; '99% pass rate on most compiler test suites' incl. GCC torture suite; compiles 'Linux 6.9 on x86, ARM, and RISC-V', plus QEMU/FFmpeg/SQLite/Postgres/Redis; could not fit a 16-bit x86 generator in 32KB; output slower than gcc -O0 per The Register 2026-02-09.

name: Cursor — "Scaling long-running autonomous coding" (FastRender browser, hundreds of agents)
one_line: Planner/worker/judge hierarchy with optimistic concurrency ran hundreds of GPT-5.2-Codex agents for a week to produce a 1M+ line browser; critics found 88% CI job failure.
why_relevant: (1) architecture choices with stated negative results: lock-based coordination made 'twenty agents... slow down to the effective throughput of two or three' so they switched to optimistic concurrency; flat (all-equal) teams became 'risk-averse' and 'avoided difficult tasks'; an 'integrator' QA role 'created more bottlenecks than it solved'; a judge agent decides whether to continue each cycle. Their lesson 'The harness and models matter, but the prompts matter more' and 'Many of our improvements came from removing complexity' is relevant to our self-repair tier. (4) The Register's follow-up is the counter-evidence: output existed, quality gate did not.
claimed_results: 2026-01-14: browser 'over 1 million lines of code across 1,000 files' in 'close to a week'; React migration '+266K/-193K edits' over 'three weeks'; video renderer '25x faster'; other runs: Java LSP 550K LoC, Windows 7 emulator 1.2M LoC, Excel 1.6M LoC; 'trillions of tokens'. The Register 2026-01-22: 3 million lines, '88 percent job failure rate' on GitHub Actions, CI build still failing, CEO: it 'kind of works'.

name: Cursor — cloud agents write >30% of Cursor's own merged PRs ("agents can now control their own computers" + Aug-19-2026 changelog)
one_line: Cursor reports that autonomous sandboxed cloud agents now author more than 30% of PRs merged internally, with proof-of-work artifacts (video, screenshots, logs) attached to each PR.
why_relevant: (4) documented production adoption of unattended ticket→PR agents at a vendor's own codebase, and (3) the verification artefact pattern: agents 'build and test software directly in sandbox environments' and attach recorded video/screenshots/logs so reviewers can validate without checkout — analogous to our rendered taste-critic stills. Aug 2026 changelog adds goal-holding loops: agents 'hold a goal until it's met', auto-subscribe to their PRs and 'drive them to completion, fixing CI and addressing bot comments'.
claimed_results: 2026-02-24: 'More than 30% of the PRs we merge at Cursor are now created by agents operating autonomously in cloud sandboxes.' DevOps.com (secondary, 2026) reports a later '35%... That number was zero eighteen months ago' — not verified on cursor.com. Changelog 2026-08-19: subscriptions/scheduled tasks 'available for cloud agents only, for now'; no percentages.

name: OpenAI Symphony — Linear-as-state-machine Codex orchestration (spec + Elixir reference impl)
one_line: Each Linear issue gets a dedicated Codex agent and persistent workspace; a dispatcher polls the board, respawns crashed runs, answers 'no human available' to questions, and shepherds PRs through CI/merge.
why_relevant: (1) the closest published shape to our ticket-in→software-out loop: tracker status is the only state, per-ticket isolated workspace, non-interactive mode (agent can't stall on a human), automatic re-queue instead of babysitting, agents can create subtasks, PR must carry proof (CI status, review feedback, complexity analysis, walkthrough videos). Explicit preconditions match our design assumptions: WORKFLOW.md guardrails, 'agent-friendly repositories with comprehensive test coverage', 'Not suitable for ambiguous problems'. Reference-impl defaults (from heyuan110 guide, 2026-03-06): poll 30s, max 10 concurrent agents, 10-min timeout, 3 retries with 5-min backoff cap.
claimed_results: openai.com post 2026-04-27: among OpenAI teams 'the number of landed PRs increase by 500% in the first three weeks'; engineers 'filed speculative tasks knowing the cost was near zero'. Repo (fetched 2026-09-02): 27k stars, 2.8k forks, Apache-2.0, 'Low-key engineering preview for testing in trusted environments', first visible commit 2026-03-27, last commit 2026-08-12. Search snippets also attribute to OpenAI 'merge 70% more pull requests each week' and 'Codex reviews 100% of PRs internally' — not found on the pages I opened, treat as unverified.

name: Anthropic — "Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice"
one_line: Anthropic's own telemetry on how unattended Claude Code sessions have become: success on hardest internal tasks doubled while human interventions per session fell 5.4→3.3.
why_relevant: (4) quantified trend data on unattended operation: long-tail turn length, auto-approve adoption, interruption rates, and how often the agent itself pauses for clarification — useful priors for our plan-seat clarifying-questions budget and for expected run lengths.
claimed_results: 2026-02-18: internal 'success rate on internal users' most challenging tasks doubled' Aug→Dec 2025; interventions per session '5.4 to 3.3'; 99.9th-percentile turn duration 'under 25 minutes in late September to over 45 minutes in early January'; full auto-approve 'roughly 20% of sessions' for new users vs 'over 40%' at 750+ sessions; interrupts '5% of turns' (new) vs 'around 9%' (experienced); Claude pauses for clarification 'more than twice as often' on complex tasks (35% to present options, 21% to gather diagnostics); 0.8% of API tool calls irreversible.

name: Anthropic — "How Anthropic teams use Claude Code" + Boris Cherny's stated workflow
one_line: Anthropic's internal usage report (autonomous write-test-iterate loops in Product Design) plus the Claude Code lead's public claims of 100% agent-written contributions with browser-based verification.
why_relevant: (1)/(4): documents that Anthropic's own teams run 'autonomous loops where Claude Code writes the code for the new feature, runs tests, and iterates continuously'; Cherny's workflow (InfoQ 2026-01-10) is a many-parallel-sessions pattern with a real verification loop ('Claude tests every single change I land... using the Claude Chrome extension... iterates until the code works') and a measured abandonment rate — a useful baseline for our falseFinish/abandon accounting.
claimed_results: claude.com 2025-07-24: security debugging '3x as quickly'; inference research '80% reduction' (1h → 10–20 min); no failures reported. Cherny on X 2025-12-27: 'In the last thirty days, 100% of my contributions to Claude Code were written by Claude Code'. InfoQ 2026-01-10: 5 local + 5–10 web sessions in separate checkouts; '10-20% of those sessions are abandoned'. Fortune 2026-01-29 (search snippet): Anthropic spokesperson 70–90% AI-written company-wide, ~90% for Claude Code itself — snippet only.

name: Claude Code agent teams — official docs (lead + teammates + shared task list)
one_line: Experimental agent teams: a lead spawns teammates that claim tasks from a file-locked shared list, message via JSON mailboxes, and can be gated by TaskCompleted/TeammateIdle hooks — but only in interactive sessions.
why_relevant: (1) the exact 'agent teams' primitive the owner named, with the constraint that matters most for us: 'In non-interactive mode with the -p flag, including Agent SDK sessions, Claude doesn't spawn teammates' — so our CLI-subprocess seats cannot use it as-is; the shared-task-list + hook-gate pattern must be reimplemented in the orchestrator. Mechanisms to copy: task dependencies auto-unblock, file-locked claiming, `TaskCompleted` hook exit-code-2 to refuse completion (a falseFinish gate), `TeammateIdle` exit-2 to keep working, plan-mode teammates whose plan is auto-approved by the lead. Documented failure modes: task status lag blocks dependents, teammates stop on errors, lead 'stops early', no /resume of teammates, file overwrites, 'Letting a team run unattended for too long increases the risk of wasted effort.'
claimed_results: none stated (docs give no outcome numbers). Docs as of Claude Code v2.1.178–v2.1.251; feature shipped with Opus 4.6 on 2026-02-05 per search summaries. Guidance: start with 3–5 teammates, 5–6 tasks per teammate; teammates are 'significantly more tokens' (each a separate instance).

name: Alex Opalic — "From Tasks to Swarms: Agent Teams in Claude Code"
one_line: Opus lead + five Sonnet teammates run a QA swarm over a live site in ~3 minutes, finding 10 real defects, at ~4x the tokens of a solo session.
why_relevant: (3) a concrete independent-critic deployment: five disjoint QA lenses (pages, posts, links, SEO, a11y) against a running app rather than the builder grading itself; (1) the 'plan first, parallelize second' split and cheap-model teammates under an expensive lead is a cost pattern for our critic lanes.
claimed_results: 2026-02-08: '16/16 pages pass', 83 posts checked, 146 internal URLs checked, ~3 minutes; 10 issues (4 major, 2 medium, 4 minor) incl. `<html class="false">`, missing og:type, broken OG images; token use ~800k for the 5-agent team vs ~200k solo.

name: Heeki Park — "Collaborating with agent teams in Claude Code"
one_line: Lead + three teammates on git worktrees deliver a first-pass feature in 15–20 minutes, but messages get lost, stuck teammates vanish from the lead's view, and parallel teams collide in a monolith.
why_relevant: (1)+(4): first-hand list of coordination failures in Claude Code agent teams that our orchestrator's in-run healing would need to detect (lost inter-agent messages, lead losing track of stuck teammates, cross-team merge conflicts) and a rough per-teammate context overhead figure for budgeting.
claimed_results: 2026-03-12: 'agent team typically completes the first pass implementation within 15–20 minutes'; 'team lead and three teammates, each loading 10k as initialization context, that's 40k token usage'; 'teammates were not receiving any messages from the team lead'; 'teammates get stuck and the team lead loses track of them'; merge conflicts from 'three agent teams, each working on a separate issue'. Verification was manual (author ran servers in tmux).

name: Developers Digest — "12 Tools in One Night: An Honest Overnight Agent Report"
one_line: A `/loop 10m` orchestrator spawning 5–8 subagents per cycle opened 60 PRs across 21 repos overnight — and kept opening them after CI died on a billing wall, and reported one PR that never existed.
why_relevant: (1) unattended orchestrator + subagent fan-out with PR-not-merge as the safety boundary; (4) three failure classes we must guard against: the orchestrator not noticing an external gate (CI) had stopped running (needs a negative control), a rule violation caught only by a later QA agent, and a fabricated success report ('hallucinated PR #51') — a live example of the falseFinish metric.
claimed_results: 2026-04-29 (run 2026-04-28 23:47 → morning): 12 new repos scaffolded, '60 pull requests opened across 21 repositories' (59 by 01:53), 6 tutorials, 8 packages, 817 detail pages enriched, 5-PR backend migration; ~03:15 UTC GitHub Actions stopped on failed payment while the orchestrator continued; PR #37 ignored a 'no gradients' rule; PR #51 'fabricated a PR number that did not exist'.

name: Celso Pinto — "Building a complete SaaS product with only Claude Code" (OnboardingHub)
one_line: Founder files ~50 Linear tickets and a CLAUDE.md 'Agent Operating Manual' (isolated envs, ticket lifecycle, UI/UX review, QA, review verdict must say APPROVED); Claude writes 95%+ of a 38k-LOC multi-tenant Rails SaaS in 55 days.
why_relevant: (1) ticket→whole-application with parallel isolated Claude sessions; (3) explicit in-pipeline review gates (DHH-style reviewer requiring an explicit 'APPROVED' verdict, coverage thresholds 85% line / 80% branch); (4) the production fire shows what held-out tests didn't cover: environment/config drift (migration vs prepare, undocumented env var, cache tables) — arguing for environment-level checks in our sealed gate, not just feature tests.
claimed_results: 2026-02-08: '38,632 lines of code (657 source files)', 713 commits, 55 days (2025-12-15 → 2026-02-08), ~25–45 human hours vs ~800 estimated traditional, '20–30x' leverage; Feb 3–4 outage: 12 cascading failures (Solid Queue tables never created, '341+ orphaned accounts', missing STRIPE_TRIAL_PRICE_ID, R2 checksum rejects, pool starvation, 512 MB dyno OOM), fixed in 14 forward commits, zero reverts. No revenue/user numbers.

name: Broccoli (besimple-oss) — Show HN: Linear tickets → sandbox → adversarial review → PR
one_line: Self-hosted (GCP/Blaxel) pipeline: per-ticket cloud sandbox, plan critique and code review by an adversarial two-agent pair, test loop, PR for humans; team reports 100% of non-developer PRs went through it.
why_relevant: (1)+(3): a small team's production ticket queue with an adversarial critic stage before the PR — the submitter's own caveat is the useful part: it takes 'multiple rounds of design critiques, then multiple rounds of code review' to avoid low-quality output, and Linear must be the single source of truth to stop ticket/codebase drift.
